 T-Mobile: We'll be first with 6G, and no to SpaceX MVNO 
 T-Mobile reports Q3 earnings and says it aims to be first with 6G in the US. It also continues to rule out an MVNO deal with SpaceX's Starlink.
 Michelle Donegan , Senior Editor, Light Reading October 29, 2026
 4 Min Read (Source: T-Mobile) T-Mobile doubled down on its physical AI network vision and claimed it will be the first carrier to launch 6G in the US on this week's third quarter earnings call. It also ruled out a SpaceX MVNO deal for consumer services as well as physical and edge AI. 
 The carrier didn't say when it would launch a 6G service but pointed to the industry expectation for a 2030 timeframe. 
 "2030 will see 6G networks being built and T-Mobile will be the first with 6G in this country with new applications like integrated sensing and communications [ISAC]. 6G will be the first G, where the basestations and radios behave as radars ... that opens up a lot of new use cases with remote sensing ... that I think is going to drive a lot of usage as well," said John Saw, chief technology officer at T-Mobile. 
 The carrier also expects cellular traffic patterns in 2030 to be different from today as AI usage increases. Saw said his mobile traffic assumption for 2030 is "still downlink heavy but increasingly uplink rich," driven by AI wearables, AI agents and "explosive growth by then of physical AI devices, like humanoids, robots, delivery drones, vehicles and factory machines." 
 Related: T-Mobile makes first AI-RAN call with Nokia and Nvidia 
 The upcoming spectrum auctions for upper C-band and 2.7GHz offer T-Mobile opportunity to add capacity for 6G as well as to boost uplink bandwidth, he noted. 
 T-Mobile gets physical
 Ahead of T-Mobile's third quarter results, Saw published a blog that explained some of the work with partners on physical AI , such as Figure AI's humanoid robots, Serve Robotics' delivery robots and 5G-connected cameras for the city of San Jose. 
 It has also teamed with Amazon Web Services to build initial instances of what it calls its "kinetic edge." This is described as bringing together T-Mobile's 5G-Advanced network and distributed edge with AWS' cloud orchestration and AI services to bring "deterministic connectivity, compute and intelligence closer to where machines operate," according to the blog. 
 T-Mobile CEO Srini Gopalan said during the earnings call that the physical AI projects show the carrier is moving beyond eSIM connectivity for humanoid robots to "testing how the network helps deliver the intelligence itself." He also admitted that physical AI is in "very early innings" for how it plays out in terms of the specific revenue opportunities, and associated costs, for telcos. 
 That said, he reckoned there is little debate about what the world will be like in 2035, as in, "whether we're going to see millions of robots, drones, all sorts of other connected moving objects. That's kind of a given when you future-cast the world. Now the question is, what kind of infrastructure do you need to support that?" 
 Related: Verizon and Ericsson make first 6G call outside in 7GHz band 
 No Musky MVNO
 T-Mobile, naturally, views its 5G-Advanced and future 6G networks as at the heart of a physical AI future. But it's space-based partner and rival SpaceX is also building a connectivity business based on expected capacity demands from robots, cars and AI agents. 
 Despite the common interest, and their existing relationship, Gopalan has not changed his position and rejects the possibility of extending an MVNO relationship to SpaceX or other satellite operators. 
 "We've been very clear that in terms of satellite, we see it as a complementary product," he said. "If we're talking about SpaceX as a customer or us being a customer of them, that's a purely commercial agreement. But the answer to the MVNO [question] is I see no room for an MVNO with SpaceX either on the consumer side or on the physical and edge AI side." 
 Q3 snapshot
 T-Mobile's Q3 results were released against a dramatic backdrop, with former CEO Mike Sievert resigning from the board and a reported reprieve from parent Deutsche Telekom's unwanted merger advances . 
 Sievert is stepping down from his role as vice chairman on the board of directors on November 1, one year after handing the reins to Gopalan. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reported that Deutsche Telekom has put on hold plans to bid for a full takeover of its US operation, partly due to opposition from its works council and from some executives within T-Mobile. 
 Related: Musk's mobile plan comes down to Earth with tower talk 
 Looking at the Q3 numbers, service revenue was up by an enviable 6% year-on-year to $19.4 billion. The growth was attributed to higher postpaid service revenue that included uptake following the acquisitions of UScellular and Metronet in Q3 last year, but partly offset by lower prepaid service revenue. Postpaid service revenue increased 9% to $16.3 billion. 
 Adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) was up 11% to $9.6 billion. 
 As for subscriber metrics, T-Mobile no longer breaks out individual net additions for mobile, fixed wireless access or fiber, and only reports accounts. The carrier added 274,000 net postpaid accounts in Q3, up 3% year-on-year for a total of 35 million. Compared to Q2, postpaid net account additions were down slightly from 277,000. It noted there was a slight decrease in net additions due to higher broadband-only customer churn and the impact from changes to the carrier's rate plan. 
 The carrier reported average revenue per account of $155.73, up 4%. Meanwhile, postpaid account churn ticked up 12 basis points to 1.09%. 
 About the Author
 Michelle Donegan
 Senior Editor, Light Reading
 Michelle Donegan covers all things 5G, 6G and mobile tech for Light Reading. She has been writing about the telecoms sector since the early 1990s. 
 Her first job was with Global Telephony magazine in Chicago, where she got an intro to publishing and tech reporting. After moving to the UK in 1999, she has covered telecoms tech, business and policy issues at publications including Communications Week International and Total Telecom. She was also part of Light Reading’s European editorial team from 2007 to 2013. Between stints at Light Reading, she was busy freelancing and was a regular contributor to Mobile Europe, Mobile World Live, TelcoTitans, TM Forum, and more.
